purpose: Naltrexone is used to help people who have stopped using opioids (like heroin or prescription painkillers) or alcohol stay free from those substances. It reduces cravings and blocks the pleasurable feelings that alcohol and opioids cause. It is not a cure, but it is a helpful tool as part of a recovery program.
how_it_works: Think of opioid receptors in your brain like locks, and opioids like heroin or alcohol as keys that open those locks to create feelings of pleasure or reward. Naltrexone works by blocking those locks so the 'key' cannot get in. This means if you drink alcohol or use opioids while taking naltrexone, you will not feel the usual high or buzz, which can help reduce the urge to use them.
common_side_effects: Nausea or upset stomach, headache, tiredness, trouble sleeping, anxiety, loss of appetite, and stomach pain. These side effects are usually mild and often improve after the first week or two.
warnings: Do not take naltrexone if you are currently using opioids or if you are in opioid withdrawal — it can cause sudden, severe withdrawal symptoms. Tell your doctor if you have liver problems, because naltrexone can affect your liver. If you ever need pain medicine for surgery or an emergency, tell your medical team you are on naltrexone, as it will block opioid pain medicines from working. Never try to overcome the blocking effect by taking large doses of opioids — this can be life-threatening.
typical_dosing: The tablet form (ReVia) is usually taken once a day, commonly as a 50 mg tablet by mouth. The injectable form (Vivitrol) is given as a shot once a month by your healthcare provider. Your doctor will decide which form and dose is right for you.
